purpose: Small frozen mathematical interfaces; expectations are test/oracle metadata and never enter model input. No original invocation events or run artifacts.

candidate.statement: Let N={1,2,3,...}. For every function K:N x N -> R such that K(a,b)=K(b,a) for all a,b in N and such that sum_{i=1}^r sum_{j=1}^r c_i c_j K(n_i,n_j)>=0 for every positive integer r, all n_1,...,n_r in N, and all c_1,...,c_r in R, there exist a real Hilbert space H and vectors v_n in H for every n in N such that <v_a,v_b>=K(a,b) for all a,b in N.
candidate.proof: Fix a function K satisfying the stated assumptions. Let V be the real vector space of all finitely supported functions x:N->R. For x,y in V define B(x,y)=sum_{a in N} sum_{b in N} x(a)y(b)K(a,b), where the sum is finite. This is a symmetric bilinear form. If the support of x is contained in {n_1,...,n_r}, the assumed inequality, after collecting coefficients at repeated indices if necessary, gives B(x,x)>=0. Let Z={x in V:B(x,x)=0}. If z is in Z and y is in V, positivity gives 0<=B(y+tz,y+tz)=B(y,y)+2tB(y,z) for every real t. If B(y,z) were nonzero, choosing t with the opposite sign and sufficiently large magnitude would make the right side negative. Hence B(y,z)=0 for every y. Thus every element of Z lies in the radical of B. It follows immediately that Z is a vector subspace: for z_1,z_2 in Z and scalars alpha,beta, the vector alpha z_1+beta z_2 is B-orthogonal to every vector, including itself. Form the quotient E=V/Z and set <x+Z,y+Z>_E=B(x,y). This is well-defined because every element of Z is B-orthogonal to V. It is symmetric and bilinear, and it is positive definite because <x+Z,x+Z>_E=0 holds exactly when x is in Z. Therefore E is a real inner-product space. Its inner product satisfies Cauchy--Schwarz: if v is nonzero, substitute t=<u,v>_E/<v,v>_E into 0<=<u-tv,u-tv>_E; the resulting inequality is |<u,v>_E|^2<=<u,u>_E<v,v>_E. The case v=0 is immediate. For completeness, construct the Hilbert-space completion explicitly. Let C be the set of Cauchy sequences (x_m) in E, and declare (x_m) equivalent to (y_m) when ||x_m-y_m||_E tends to zero. Let H be the set of equivalence classes. Addition and scalar multiplication are defined termwise, and define <[(x_m)],[(y_m)]>_H=lim_{m->infinity}<x_m,y_m>_E. The limit exists: Cauchy sequences are bounded, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives |<x_m,y_m>_E-<x_l,y_l>_E|<=||x_m-x_l||_E ||y_m||_E+||x_l||_E ||y_m-y_l||_E, which tends to zero as m,l tend to infinity. The same estimate shows independence of representatives. The resulting form is an inner product: in particular, if its value on [(x_m)] with itself is zero, then ||x_m||_E tends to zero, so (x_m) is equivalent to the zero sequence. The space H is complete. Indeed, embed E isometrically into H by j(x)=[(x,x,...)]. This image is dense because for X=[(x_m)], the distance from X to j(x_m) tends to zero. Now let (X_k) be Cauchy in H. Choose increasing indices k_m such that ||X_k-X_l||_H<2^{-m} whenever k,l>=k_m, and use density to choose x_m in E with ||j(x_m)-X_{k_m}||_H<2^{-m}. Then ||x_{m+1}-x_m||_E<=2^{-(m+1)}+2^{-m}+2^{-m}. Consequently (x_m) is Cauchy in E. Put X=[(x_m)] in H. The displayed summable bound shows ||j(x_m)-X||_H tends to zero, and hence ||X_{k_m}-X||_H tends to zero. Since (X_k) is Cauchy and has a subsequence converging to X, the entire sequence converges to X. Thus H is a real Hilbert space. For n in N, let e_n in V be the function equal to 1 at n and 0 elsewhere, and set v_n=j(e_n+Z). Then for every a,b in N, <v_a,v_b>_H=<e_a+Z,e_b+Z>_E=B(e_a,e_b)=K(a,b). This supplies the required Hilbert space and vectors.

candidate.statement: Let N be a positive integer, let p<=N be prime, and let lambda_1,...,lambda_N be nonnegative real numbers with sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M=1. For every positive integer r define H(r)=sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M floor(M/r), and let K=max{M:lambda_M>0}. Let x,y,z be real numbers such that G=[[x,y],[y,z]] is positive semidefinite. For 1<=i,j<=N define Z_{i,j}=sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M 1_{i<=M}1_{j<=M}[x+y(1_{p|i}+1_{p|j})+z1_{p|i}1_{p|j}]. Then Z is positive semidefinite, trace(Z)=xH(1)+(2y+z)H(p), and, for every coprime pair 1<=a<b<=N, sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=xH(b)+(2y+z)H(bp) if p does not divide ab, while sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=(x+y)H(b)+(y+z)H(bp) if exactly one of a,b is divisible by p. Suppose additionally that sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=H(b) for every such coprime pair. Set T=trace(Z). Then the feasible coefficients and trace satisfy the following classification. If K=1, there are no effective class equations and T=x>=0. If 2<=K<p, then x=1 and T=H(1). If p=K=2 and t=lambda_2, then x+y=1, x>0, z>=(1-x)^2/x, and T>=2sqrt(t), with equality attainable; hence H(1)-T<=(1-sqrt(t))^2<1. In every remaining case K>=p, one has x=1, y=0 and T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1); moreover z=0 if K>=2p, while the class equations impose no additional restriction on z when K<2p. Consequently H(1)-T<=1 in every case. Finally, define c=H(p)/H(1) and delta_b=H(bp)-cH(b). For every applicable class with H(b)>0, a no-divisibility equation implies (H(1)-T)/H(1)=(2y+z)delta_b/H(b), and an exactly-one-divisibility equation implies (H(1)-T)/H(1)=(1-c)y+(y+z)delta_b/H(b). In particular, exact scale invariance delta_b=0 on a no-divisibility class forces T=H(1).
candidate.proof: For n>=1 put f(n)=(1,1_{p|n})^T. The displayed entry is Z_{i,j}=sum_M lambda_M 1_{i<=M}1_{j<=M} f(i)^T G f(j). For every v in R^N, v^T Z v=sum_M lambda_M (sum_{i<=M}v_i f(i))^T G(sum_{i<=M}v_i f(i))>=0, so Z is positive semidefinite. On the diagonal, f(n)^TGf(n)=x+(2y+z)1_{p|n}. Therefore trace(Z)=sum_M lambda_M[xM+(2y+z)floor(M/p)]=xH(1)+(2y+z)H(p). Fix coprime a<b and M. Since qa<qb, both qa and qb are at most M exactly when q<=floor(M/b). If p does not divide ab, then p divides qa exactly when p divides q, and the same is true of qb. Thus f(qa)^TGf(qb) equals x when p does not divide q and x+2y+z when p divides q. The sum over q<=floor(M/b) is x floor(M/b)+(2y+z)floor(M/(bp)). Averaging over M proves the first class formula. Since a and b are coprime, at most one is divisible by p. If exactly one is divisible by p, one of the two divisibility indicators is always 1 and the other equals 1_{p|q}. The summand is consequently x+y+(y+z)1_{p|q}, whose sum and average give the second formula. Because lambda_K>0, H(b)>0 exactly when b<=K. Also floor(M/(bp))=floor(floor(M/b)/p), so 0<=H(bp)<=H(b)/p<H(b) whenever H(b)>0. A no-divisibility class exists for every 2<=b<=K with p not dividing b, by taking a=1. An exactly-one-divisibility class exists for every p<=b<=K: take a=1 when p divides b, and take a=p when b>p and p does not divide b. If K=1, both H(b) and H(bp) vanish for every b>=2, so all class equations are automatic. Here H(1)=1, H(p)=0 and T=x>=0 because G is positive semidefinite. Suppose 2<=K<p. Every effective class is a no-divisibility class and H(bp)=0. Taking b=2 in the first equation gives xH(2)=H(2), hence x=1. Since H(p)=0, T=H(1). Suppose K=p>=3. The no-divisibility equation at b=2 has H(2p)=0 and gives x=1. At b=p the exactly-one equation has H(p^2)=0 and gives x+y=1, hence y=0. Positive semidefiniteness gives z>=0, so T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1). Suppose K>=p+1. At b=p+1, a=1 supplies a no-divisibility equation and a=p supplies an exactly-one equation. Subtracting these equations gives y[H(p(p+1))-H(p+1)]=0. The bracket is strictly negative, so y=0. For every 2<=b<=K at least one of the two class types exists; its equation now reads xH(b)+zH(bp)=H(b). Taking b=K and using H(Kp)=0 gives x=1. Hence T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1). If K>=2p, then H(2p)>0, and the equation at b=2 forces z=0. If K<2p, then H(bp)=0 for every b>=2, so after x=1 and y=0 the class equations place no further restriction on z. It remains to treat p=K=2. Put t=lambda_2; then 0<t<=1, H(1)=1+t, H(2)=t, and H(4)=0. The only effective class has (a,b)=(1,2), and its equation is x+y=1. If x=0, positive semidefiniteness would force y=0, contradicting this equation; hence x>0. The quadratic form of G is nonnegative only if z>=y^2/x=(1-x)^2/x. Conversely this inequality makes x r^2+2yrs+zs^2=x(r+ys/x)^2+(z-y^2/x)s^2 nonnegative, so it is also sufficient. Therefore T=x(1+t)+[2(1-x)+z]t >=x(1+t)+[2(1-x)+(1-x)^2/x]t =x+t/x >=2sqrt(t), where the last inequality follows from x+t/x-2sqrt(t)=(sqrt(x)-sqrt(t/x))^2. Equality holds for x=sqrt(t), y=1-sqrt(t), z=(1-sqrt(t))^2/sqrt(t). Since H(1)=1+t, the maximal saving is 1+t-2sqrt(t)=(1-sqrt(t))^2<1. Combining the cases gives H(1)-T<=1. Finally c=H(p)/H(1) is well-defined and c<1 because H(p)<=H(1)/p. Write H(bp)=cH(b)+delta_b. In a no-divisibility equation, substitution gives x+c(2y+z)=1-(2y+z)delta_b/H(b). The left side is T/H(1), proving the first defect identity. In an exactly-one equation, substitution gives x=1-y-c(y+z)-(y+z)delta_b/H(b). Adding c(2y+z) to both sides and subtracting from 1 proves the second identity. If delta_b=0 in a no-divisibility class, the first identity gives T=H(1).

candidate.statement: The conjunction of these statements ["Prove that for every real number A>=2 there exist positive integers N and L, nonnegative real numbers lambda_1,...,lambda_N with sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M=1, real numbers alpha_1,...,alpha_N, vectors z_1,...,z_L in R^N, and real numbers beta_{a,b,q} indexed by all triples of positive integers (a,b,q) satisfying qa<=N and qb<=N, such that sum_{i=1}^N alpha_i>A^2 and the following identity of real symmetric N by N matrices holds. Let e_1,...,e_N be the standard basis of R^N; for 1<=M<=N define u_M=sum_{i=1}^M e_i; and for 1<=i,j<=N define E_{i,j}=(e_i e_j^T+e_j e_i^T)/2. Then sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M u_M u_M^T = sum_{ell=1}^L z_ell z_ell^T + sum_{i=1}^N alpha_i e_i e_i^T + sum_{(a,b,q): qa<=N, qb<=N} beta_{a,b,q}(E_{qa,qb}-E_{a,b})."] implies the statement "Let N={1,2,3,...}. Prove that for every real number A>=2 and every function K:N x N -> R satisfying K(a,b)=K(b,a), K(a,a)=1, and K(qa,qb)=K(a,b) for all positive integers a,b,q, and satisfying sum_{i=1}^r sum_{j=1}^r c_i c_j K(n_i,n_j)>=0 for every positive integer r, all positive integers n_1,...,n_r, and all real numbers c_1,...,c_r, there exists a positive integer M such that sum_{a=1}^M sum_{b=1}^M K(a,b)>A^2.".
candidate.proof: Assume the stated certificate requirement. Fix A and K satisfying every hypothesis in the conclusion, and take N,L, lambda_M, alpha_i, beta_{a,b,q}, and z_l supplied by the requirement. Define the real symmetric N by N matrix G by G_ab=K(a,b). It is positive semidefinite by applying the assumed kernel inequality with r=N, n_i=i, and arbitrary real c_i. Use the Frobenius pairing <X,Y>=sum_{i,j=1}^N X_ij Y_ij. For the objects in the requirement, <u_M u_M^T,G>=sum_{a,b<=M}K(a,b), <e_i e_i^T,G>=K(i,i)=1, and <E_ij,G>=G_ij. Therefore every dilation-relation term has pairing <E_{qa,qb}-E_{a,b},G>=K(qa,qb)-K(a,b)=0. Moreover, <z_l z_l^T,G>=z_l^T G z_l>=0 because G is positive semidefinite. Pairing the certificate identity with G consequently gives sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M sum_{a=1}^M sum_{b=1}^M K(a,b) >= sum_{i=1}^N alpha_i>A^2. The lambda_M are nonnegative and sum to 1. If every displayed kernel sum for M<=N were at most A^2, their lambda-weighted average would be at most A^2, a contradiction. Hence at least one positive integer M<=N has sum_{a,b<=M}K(a,b)>A^2, as required.

candidate.statement: Let N be a positive integer and let lambda_1,...,lambda_N be nonnegative real numbers with sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M=1. Define H(k)=sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M floor(M/k) for every positive integer k, and let K=max{M:lambda_M>0}. For n>=1 put v(n)=(1,1_{2|n},1_{3|n}) in R^3. Let G=[[x,y,z],[y,r,s],[z,s,w]] be a real positive-semidefinite matrix, and for 1<=i,j<=N define Z_{i,j}=sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M 1_{i<=M}1_{j<=M} v(i)^T Gv(j). Suppose that sum_{q<=N/b} Z_{qa,qb}=H(b) for every coprime pair 1<=a<b<=N, and put T=trace(Z). Then Z is positive semidefinite and T=xH(1)+(2y+r)H(2)+(2z+w)H(3)+2sH(6). For an effective coprime class a<b, put h=H(b), h_2=H(2b), h_3=H(3b), and h_6=H(6b). According as neither prime divides either endpoint, exactly the prime 2 divides one endpoint, exactly the prime 3 divides one endpoint, both primes divide the same endpoint, or the primes divide opposite endpoints, the class equation has respective coefficient row for (x,y,z,r,s,w): (h,2h_2,2h_3,h_2,2h_6,h_3), (h,h+h_2,2h_3,h_2,h_3+h_6,h_3), (h,2h_2,h+h_3,h_2,h_2+h_6,h_3), (h,h+h_2,h+h_3,h_2,h_2+h_3,h_3), or (h,h+h_2,h+h_3,h_2,h+h_6,h_3), and the scalar product of that row with (x,y,z,r,s,w) equals h. The feasible matrices and minimum trace are classified as follows. If K=1, then T=x>=0. If K=2 and theta=lambda_2, then the effective upper-left 2-by-2 block satisfies x+y=1, x>0 and r>=(1-x)^2/x, and T>=2sqrt(theta), with equality attainable. If K=3, put P=H(2) and Q=H(3). Then y=z=1-x and s=x-1; writing c=(1-x)^2/x, positive semidefiniteness is equivalent to x>0, r>=c, w>=c and (r-c)(w-c)>=(1-x)^2/x^2. In this case the minimum trace is H(1) when sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q)>=1 and is 2(sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q))-2sqrt(PQ) when sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q)<=1; both minima are attainable. If K=4, every feasible matrix has the form G=[[1+rho,-rho,-rho],[-rho,rho,rho],[-rho,rho,w]] with rho>=0 and w>=rho, and T=H(1)+rho+(w-rho)H(3)>=H(1). If K=5, then G=diag(1,0,w) with w>=0 and T=H(1)+wH(3)>=H(1). If K>=6, then G=diag(1,0,0) and T=H(1). Consequently H(1)-T<=1 in every case; for K=3 its exact maximum over feasible G is max{0,(1-sqrt(H(2))-sqrt(H(3)))^2}<1.
candidate.proof: For any real numbers c_1,...,c_N, sum_{i,j}c_iZ_{i,j}c_j=sum_M lambda_M (sum_{i<=M}c_iv(i))^T G(sum_{j<=M}c_jv(j))>=0, so Z is positive semidefinite. Since v(i)^TGv(i)=x+(2y+r)1_{2|i}+(2z+w)1_{3|i}+2s1_{6|i}, summing the diagonal first over i<=M and then over M gives the asserted trace formula. Fix coprime a<b. Because qa<qb, both cutoff indicators in Z_{qa,qb} equal 1 precisely when qb<=M. Thus sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=sum_M lambda_M sum_{q<=M/b}v(qa)^TGv(qb). For p in {2,3}, coprimality prevents p from dividing both a and b. If p divides neither, both p-coordinates in the bilinear expression equal 1_{p|q}; if p divides one endpoint, those coordinates are 1 and 1_{p|q}. Hence the diagonal coefficient r always sums to H(2b), and w always sums to H(3b). The y coefficient is 2H(2b) when 2 divides neither endpoint and H(b)+H(2b) otherwise; the z coefficient is analogous. If neither prime divides either endpoint, the s term is 2 times 1_{6|q}. If only 2 occurs at an endpoint it is 1_{3|q}+1_{6|q}; if only 3 occurs it is 1_{2|q}+1_{6|q}. When both occur at the same endpoint it is 1_{2|q}+1_{3|q}, and when they occur at opposite endpoints it is 1+1_{6|q}. Summation gives exactly the five displayed rows. A class is effective exactly when b<=K. Its possible rows can be read off using small coprime choices of a. For b=2 only the 2-state occurs. If b is an odd multiple of 3, a=1 and a=2 produce the 3-only and opposite-endpoint states. If b>=4 is even and not divisible by 3, a=1 and a=3 produce the 2-only and opposite-endpoint states. If b>=5 is coprime to 6, a=1,2,3 produce the 00, 2-only and 3-only states; a=6 additionally produces the same-endpoint state when b>=7. If 6 divides b, every admissible a is coprime to 6 and only the same-endpoint state occurs. These choices also show that the list is exhaustive. Comparing the two rows at an effective odd multiple b of 3 gives (H(b)-H(2b))(y+s)=0. The coefficient is positive: for each M, floor(M/b)-floor(M/(2b)) counts odd positive integers at most M/b, and the term M=K contributes positively. Hence y+s=0. Similarly, comparison at an effective even nonmultiple b of 3 gives z+s=0. At an effective b>=5 coprime to 6, comparison of the 00 row with the 2-only and 3-only rows gives (H(b)-H(2b))y+(H(3b)-H(6b))s=0, (H(b)-H(3b))z+(H(2b)-H(6b))s=0. Also R_b=H(b)-H(2b)-H(3b)+H(6b)>0, because for each M its summand counts positive integers at most M/b divisible by neither 2 nor 3, and the M=K summand contains 1 whenever b<=K. Suppose K>=5. The comparisons at b=3 and b=4 give y=z=-s. Substitution into the first comparison at b=5 gives -sR_5=0, so s=0 and therefore y=z=0. Every class equation now reduces to xH(b)+rH(2b)+wH(3b)=H(b). The terminal equation b=K gives x=1. The equation b=2 then gives rH(4)+wH(6)=0. Positive semidefiniteness gives r,w>=0, while H(4)>0 for K>=5. Thus r=0. If K>=6, then H(6)>0 and w=0, proving the stated K>=6 classification. If K=5, H(6)=0 and no class equation contains w; hence G=diag(1,0,w), w>=0. The trace conclusions follow immediately. Now let K=4. At b=3, the two equations reduce to x+z=1 and y+s=0, because every H(k) with k>4 vanishes. At b=4 they similarly give x+y=1 and z+s=0. Consequently y=z=1-x and s=x-1. At b=2, where H(4)>0 and H(6)=0, the remaining equation gives r=x-1. Put rho=x-1. Thus G=[[1+rho,-rho,-rho],[-rho,rho,rho],[-rho,rho,w]]. Necessarily rho>=0 from its second diagonal entry, and the principal minor on coordinates 2 and 3 gives rho(w-rho)>=0; together with w>=0 this says w>=rho. Conversely G=e_1e_1^T+rho(1,-1,-1)(1,-1,-1)^T+(w-rho)e_3e_3^T, so these conditions are sufficient. Since H(6)=0, T=(1+rho)H(1)-rho H(2)+(w-2rho)H(3). For support in {1,2,3,4}, direct expansion using sum_M lambda_M=1 gives H(1)-H(2)-2H(3)=1-H(3). Therefore T=H(1)+rho+(w-rho)H(3)>=H(1). Let K=3. The b=2 equation is x+y=1. At b=3, the 3-only equation is x+z=1 and comparison with the opposite-endpoint equation gives y+s=0. Hence, with d=1-x, y=z=d and s=-d. Since the principal minor on coordinates 1 and 2 would be negative if x=0, one has x>0. Completing the square in the quadratic form of G shows that G is positive semidefinite exactly when its Schur complement after the first coordinate is positive semidefinite. Put c=d^2/x. That complement is [[r-c,-d/x],[-d/x,w-c]], because d+c=d/x. A real symmetric 2-by-2 matrix [[A,k],[k,B]] is positive semidefinite exactly when A>=0, B>=0 and AB>=k^2: necessity follows from its diagonal entries and determinant, while sufficiency follows by completing the square when A>0, with the zero case immediate. This proves the stated constraints on r and w. Set P=H(2)=lambda_2+lambda_3 and Q=H(3)=lambda_3. Then P>=Q>0 and H(1)=1+P+Q. For fixed x, write A=r-c and B=w-c. The trace is T=xH(1)+2d(P+Q)+Pr+Qw. Under A,B>=0 and AB>=d^2/x^2, PA+QB>=2sqrt(PQAB)>=2|d|sqrt(PQ)/x, with equality at A=|d|sqrt(Q/P)/x and B=|d|sqrt(P/Q)/x. Consequently the minimum for fixed x is f(x)=x+(P+Q)/x+2sqrt(PQ)|1-x|/x. For x>=1 this equals x+2sqrt(PQ)+(sqrt(P)-sqrt(Q))^2/x. Since (sqrt(P)-sqrt(Q))^2<1, it is minimized on that interval at x=1. For 0<x<=1 it equals x-2sqrt(PQ)+(sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q))^2/x. If sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q)<=1, completing the square, or differentiating this elementary expression, shows that its minimum occurs at x=sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q), with value 2(sqrt(P)+sqrt(Q))-2sqrt(PQ). If the sum of square roots is at least 1, the expression decreases up to x=1 and its minimum is f(1)=1+P+Q=H(1). The displayed choices of A and B produce positive-semidefinite equality matrices, so both bounds are attained. Subtracting the first minimum from H(1) gives (1-sqrt(P)-sqrt(Q))^2. If K=2, the third coordinate of v(i) vanishes wherever Z can be nonzero. The effective construction, class equation and trace therefore coincide with the p=2 construction for the upper-left principal block [[x,y],[y,r]], which is positive semidefinite. Fact d6af36620d7472cb gives x+y=1, x>0, r>=(1-x)^2/x and T>=2sqrt(lambda_2), with equality attainable; adjoining a zero third row and column preserves equality. If K=1, lambda_1=1, there are no effective class equations, and T=x>=0 directly. For K=1 the saving is at most H(1)=1. For K=2 it is (1-sqrt(lambda_2))^2<1 by the cited fact. For K=3 it is either zero or (1-sqrt(P)-sqrt(Q))^2<1 because Q>0. For K>=4 it is nonpositive. This proves H(1)-T<=1 in all cases.

In every remaining case K>=p, one has x=1, y=0 and T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1); moreover z=0 if K>=2p, while the class equations impose no additional restriction on z when K<2p. Consequently H(1)-T<=1 in every case. Finally, define c=H(p)/H(1) and delta_b=H(bp)-cH(b). For every applicable class with H(b)>0, a no-divisibility equation implies (H(1)-T)/H(1)=(2y+z)delta_b/H(b), and an exactly-one-divisibility equation implies (H(1)-T)/H(1)=(1-c)y+(y+z)delta_b/H(b). In particular, exact scale invariance delta_b=0 on a no-divisibility class forces T=H(1).
predecessors.proof: For n>=1 put f(n)=(1,1_{p|n})^T. The displayed entry is Z_{i,j}=sum_M lambda_M 1_{i<=M}1_{j<=M} f(i)^T G f(j). For every v in R^N, v^T Z v=sum_M lambda_M (sum_{i<=M}v_i f(i))^T G(sum_{i<=M}v_i f(i))>=0, so Z is positive semidefinite. On the diagonal, f(n)^TGf(n)=x+(2y+z)1_{p|n}. Therefore trace(Z)=sum_M lambda_M[xM+(2y+z)floor(M/p)]=xH(1)+(2y+z)H(p). Fix coprime a<b and M. Since qa<qb, both qa and qb are at most M exactly when q<=floor(M/b). If p does not divide ab, then p divides qa exactly when p divides q, and the same is true of qb. Thus f(qa)^TGf(qb) equals x when p does not divide q and x+2y+z when p divides q. The sum over q<=floor(M/b) is x floor(M/b)+(2y+z)floor(M/(bp)). Averaging over M proves the first class formula. Since a and b are coprime, at most one is divisible by p. If exactly one is divisible by p, one of the two divisibility indicators is always 1 and the other equals 1_{p|q}. The summand is consequently x+y+(y+z)1_{p|q}, whose sum and average give the second formula. Because lambda_K>0, H(b)>0 exactly when b<=K. Also floor(M/(bp))=floor(floor(M/b)/p), so 0<=H(bp)<=H(b)/p<H(b) whenever H(b)>0. A no-divisibility class exists for every 2<=b<=K with p not dividing b, by taking a=1. An exactly-one-divisibility class exists for every p<=b<=K: take a=1 when p divides b, and take a=p when b>p and p does not divide b. If K=1, both H(b) and H(bp) vanish for every b>=2, so all class equations are automatic. Here H(1)=1, H(p)=0 and T=x>=0 because G is positive semidefinite. Suppose 2<=K<p. Every effective class is a no-divisibility class and H(bp)=0. Taking b=2 in the first equation gives xH(2)=H(2), hence x=1. Since H(p)=0, T=H(1). Suppose K=p>=3. The no-divisibility equation at b=2 has H(2p)=0 and gives x=1. At b=p the exactly-one equation has H(p^2)=0 and gives x+y=1, hence y=0. Positive semidefiniteness gives z>=0, so T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1). Suppose K>=p+1. At b=p+1, a=1 supplies a no-divisibility equation and a=p supplies an exactly-one equation. Subtracting these equations gives y[H(p(p+1))-H(p+1)]=0. The bracket is strictly negative, so y=0. For every 2<=b<=K at least one of the two class types exists; its equation now reads xH(b)+zH(bp)=H(b). Taking b=K and using H(Kp)=0 gives x=1. Hence T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1). If K>=2p, then H(2p)>0, and the equation at b=2 forces z=0. If K<2p, then H(bp)=0 for every b>=2, so after x=1 and y=0 the class equations place no further restriction on z. It remains to treat p=K=2. Put t=lambda_2; then 0<t<=1, H(1)=1+t, H(2)=t, and H(4)=0. The only effective class has (a,b)=(1,2), and its equation is x+y=1. If x=0, positive semidefiniteness would force y=0, contradicting this equation; hence x>0. The quadratic form of G is nonnegative only if z>=y^2/x=(1-x)^2/x. Conversely this inequality makes x r^2+2yrs+zs^2=x(r+ys/x)^2+(z-y^2/x)s^2 nonnegative, so it is also sufficient. Therefore T=x(1+t)+[2(1-x)+z]t >=x(1+t)+[2(1-x)+(1-x)^2/x]t =x+t/x >=2sqrt(t), where the last inequality follows from x+t/x-2sqrt(t)=(sqrt(x)-sqrt(t/x))^2. Equality holds for x=sqrt(t), y=1-sqrt(t), z=(1-sqrt(t))^2/sqrt(t). Since H(1)=1+t, the maximal saving is 1+t-2sqrt(t)=(1-sqrt(t))^2<1. Combining the cases gives H(1)-T<=1. Finally c=H(p)/H(1) is well-defined and c<1 because H(p)<=H(1)/p. Write H(bp)=cH(b)+delta_b. In a no-divisibility equation, substitution gives x+c(2y+z)=1-(2y+z)delta_b/H(b). The left side is T/H(1), proving the first defect identity. In an exactly-one equation, substitution gives x=1-y-c(y+z)-(y+z)delta_b/H(b). Adding c(2y+z) to both sides and subtracting from 1 proves the second identity. If delta_b=0 in a no-divisibility class, the first identity gives T=H(1).

candidate.statement: Let N={1,2,3,...}. For every function K:N x N -> R such that K(a,b)=K(b,a) for all a,b in N, there exist a real Hilbert space H and vectors v_n in H for every n in N such that <v_a,v_b>=K(a,b) for all a,b in N.

cases.variant_description: Remove the positive-semidefinite hypothesis; symmetric negative diagonal kernel is permitted.

candidate.statement: There exist a real Hilbert space H and vectors v_n in H for every positive integer n such that for every real symmetric positive semidefinite kernel K on the positive integers, <v_a,v_b>=K(a,b) for all positive integers a,b. Here positive semidefinite means sum_{i,j=1}^r c_i c_j K(n_i,n_j)>=0 for every positive integer r, all positive integers n_i, and all real c_i.

cases.variant_description: Exchange the universal kernel and existential representation quantifiers.

candidate.statement: Let N be a positive integer, let p<=N be prime, and let lambda_1,...,lambda_N be nonnegative real numbers with sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M=1. For every positive integer r define H(r)=sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M floor(M/r), and let K=max{M:lambda_M>0}. Let x,y,z be real numbers such that G=[[x,y],[y,z]] is positive semidefinite. For 1<=i,j<=N define Z_{i,j}=sum_{M=1}^N lambda_M 1_{i<=M}1_{j<=M}[x+y(1_{p|i}+1_{p|j})+z1_{p|i}1_{p|j}]. Then Z is positive semidefinite, trace(Z)=xH(1)+(2y+z)H(p), and, for every coprime pair 1<=a<b<=N, sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=xH(b)+(2y+z)H(bp) if p does not divide ab, while sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=(x+y)H(b)+(y+z)H(bp) if exactly one of a,b is divisible by p. Suppose additionally that sum_{q<=N/b}Z_{qa,qb}=H(b) for every such coprime pair. Set T=trace(Z). Then the feasible coefficients and trace satisfy the following classification. If K=1, there are no effective class equations and T=x>=0. If 2<=K<p, then x=1 and T=H(1). If p=K=2 and t=lambda_2, then x+y=1, x>0, z>=(1-x)^2/x, and T>=2sqrt(t), with equality attainable; hence H(1)-T<=(1-sqrt(t))^2<1. In every remaining case K>=p, one has x=1, y=0 and T=H(1)+zH(p)>=H(1); moreover z=0 if K>=2p, while the class equations impose no additional restriction on z when K<2p. Consequently H(1)-T<1 in every case. Finally, define c=H(p)/H(1) and delta_b=H(bp)-cH(b). For every applicable class with H(b)>0, a no-divisibility equation implies (H(1)-T)/H(1)=(2y+z)delta_b/H(b), and an exactly-one-divisibility equation implies (H(1)-T)/H(1)=(1-c)y+(y+z)delta_b/H(b). In particular, exact scale invariance delta_b=0 on a no-divisibility class forces T=H(1).
